input.question: When did the concept of basic training come about in the military? Like the whole sergeant screaming in your face thing.
input.ground_truth: The 'sergeant screaming in your face' type of basic training largely emerged after the Second World War. S.L.A. Marshall's research during and after the Second World War found that 75 to 80 percent of riflemen *did not* fire their weapons at an exposed enemy. "When [he] was sent to the Korean War to make the same kind of investigation [...] he found that (as a result of new training techniques initiated in response to his earlier findings) 55 percent of infantrymen were firing their weapons - and in some perimeter-defense crises, almost everyone was. These training techniques were further perfected, and in Vietnam the firing rate appears to have been around 90 to 95 percent." A lot of these new training techniques involved the desensitization and conditioning that come with variations on the 'screaming in your face' style of training. If you are interested in this kind of thing, I would highly recommend Lt. Col Dave Grossman's *On Killing: The Psychological Cost of Learning to Kill in War and Society*.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: When did the concept of basic training come about in the military? Like the whole sergeant screaming in your face thing.

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine a long, long time ago, people who wanted to be soldiers didn’t really know how to work together or follow rules. So, a long time ago, someone thought, “Hey! Let’s have a special place where new soldiers can learn how to march, listen, and work as a team.”

This special place is called “basic training.” In basic training, the teachers (called drill sergeants) are very loud and strict. They shout and tell the new soldiers what to do, over and over, so everyone learns the same way and becomes a good team.

This idea started a long, long time ago—like when there were wars with big armies, maybe even in the 1800s or earlier. But it became really important when armies got bigger and needed everyone to act the same way. That’s why you see drill sergeants yelling and teaching in movies—it’s to make sure everyone learns quickly and becomes a strong team!

So, the “yelling sergeant” thing is just a way to help new soldiers learn fast and be brave and work together.
